question: A 17-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a knife fight. He initially refused to come to the hospital, but one of his wounds overlying the right antecubital fossa would not stop bleeding. Vitals include: BP 90/65, HR 115, and RR 24. He reports that he is light-headed and having visual changes. You hold direct pressure over the wound on his right arm while the rest of the team resuscitates him with crystalloid and pRBCs. After his vitals signs normalize, you note that his right arm is cool and you are unable to palpate a radial pulse. The vascular surgery team explores his right arm, finding and repairing a lacerated brachial artery. Two hours post-operatively he is complaining of 10/10 pain in his right forearm and screams out loud when you passively move his fingers. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Lacerated brachial artery repair" -> "Post-operative pain in right forearm" -> "Pain worsens with passive finger movement" -> "Possible compartment syndrome" -> "Measure forearm compartment pressures" -> 80% CHAIN: "Lacerated brachial artery repair" -> "Post-operative pain in right forearm" -> "Pain worsens with passive finger movement" -> "Possible nerve compression" -> "Consider nerve block" -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's post-operative pain in the right forearm, worsening with passive finger movement, raises concern for compartment syndrome. The most appropriate next step in management is to measure forearm compartment pressures to assess for compartment syndrome.
analysis: The patient's presentation with severe pain in the right forearm, exacerbated by passive finger movement, is concerning for compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency. The most appropriate next step in management, supported by consensus and the enhanced information provided, is to measure forearm compartment pressures to definitively diagnose compartment syndrome.
